# AGENTS.md

Conventions for AI agents and contributors in this repository. Keep it
factual: paths, commands, invariants — no essays.

## Project layout

- `lib/` — the `flutter_agent_harness` package (pure Dart core). `test/`
  mirrors it. `prompts/` — all LLM prompts as Markdown (see rules below).
- `lib/flutter_agent_harness.dart` (the barrel) — gh-1232 policy:
  GROUPED APPEND-ONLY export sections, one `// ── <subsystem> ──` comment
  header per group, exports sorted by path within a group, new exports
  appended to their subsystem group (a new subsystem starts a new group).
  No per-subsystem mini-barrels, no re-sorting of existing lines — append
  only, so parallel edits almost never touch the same line.
- God-file ceiling (gh-1232): no Dart file over 2800 lines anywhere
  (`scripts/ci_fast_gate.sh` stage_size + ci.yml guard, both covering
  `lib test example bin flutter_app/lib`). Target < 2000 for primary
  files; when a file approaches it, split by concern into `part` files
  (the established pattern: `agent_cli.dart`, `builtin_tools.dart`,
  `bin/fah.dart` → `bin/fah_*.dart`, `agent_service.dart` →
  `agent_service_*.dart` mixins) — never by extracting public API.
- `lib/src/approval/` — tool approval gate: tiers (read/write/exec),
  session modes (always-ask/write/yolo/autopilot — the CLI label of the
  `unattended` enum), per-tool overrides,
  critical-pattern
  `bash` interceptor, per-turn grants (`grantForTurn(allow:, deny:)` —
  skill `allowed-tools`/`disallowed-tools` manifest keys ride these for one
  turn; explicit deny > turnDeny > per-tool override > turnAllow >
  alwaysAllow > mode (critical bash outranks mode in always-ask/write/yolo,
  but is skipped in unattended so the mode never blocks — for runs with no
  user present); `clearTurnGrants()`
  on every new user
  message). Wired via `attachApproval` into `beforeToolCall` (runs
  first); prompt UI is an injectable `ApprovalPrompt` (null + prompt policy
  = deny).
- `lib/src/tools/ask_tool.dart` — `ask` tool: structured mid-turn questions
  via injectable `AskCallback` (null = error, cancel = plain result).
- `lib/src/tools/request_secret_tool.dart` — `request_secret` tool: the agent
  asks the USER for a missing credential via injectable
  `RequestSecretCallback` (never in chat text); a grant returns
  `RequestSecretResult` (host-adjusted `name`, `value`, `persisted` flag),
  a decline is a plain result. The app wires it in `AgentService` to
  `secretRequestHandler` (chat screen installs
  `ui/widgets/secret_request_sheet.dart`): a grant is persisted into
  `SessionKeysStore`, injected into the live shell env via
  `SecretsExecutionEnv.addSecrets` (the map is runtime-mutable now), and
  registered into the same `SecretRedactor` — so the next run's prompt name
  list, bash `$NAME`, and redaction all pick it up.
- `lib/src/env/session_vars_execution_env.dart` — `SessionVarsExecutionEnv`:
  an `ExecutionEnv` decorator injecting session-correlation env vars
  (`FAH_SESSION_ID`/`FAH_SESSION_FILE`/`FAH_PROVIDER`/`FAH_MODEL`, resolved
  live per `exec`, never secrets) into bash tool executions. Wired around
  `builtinTools` in the CLI (`AgentCli`) and the app (`AgentService`).
  `LocalShell` merges `ShellExecOptions.env` OVER `Platform.environment`
  (never replaces), so injected vars keep the inherited environment.
- `lib/src/env/io_execution_env.dart` — `LocalShell`: foreground `exec`
  runs under `setsid` when the host has it (probe
  `ownProcessGroupAvailable`, seam `ownProcessGroupOverride`) and the
  timeout/cancel paths reap the whole tree (`killTree` + direct-kill
  backstop) with a capped pipe-drain (`_drainGrace`) — timeout/cancel'd
  calls complete in ≤ timeout + kill grace + drain grace; a no-timeout
  call within `_drainGrace` of the direct child's exit (the drain is
  capped unconditionally: after the child is reaped every remaining pipe
  byte comes from an orphan). Killed calls are marked `timeout`/`aborted`
  and carry the captured partial output on `ExecutionError.stdout`/
  `stderr` — tail-capped at the source to the last 64 KiB (`_captureTail`)
  — rendered by the bash tool and the skill renderer's `!cmd` failure
  branch (every string that branch embeds is tail-capped to ~2 KB)
  (gh-1053; the timeout timer stays
  armed after the child exits because an orphaned descendant can hold
  the pipes — a drain that outlives the deadline marks the call
  `timedOut` even when the child exited 0). Background jobs (issue #517)
  keep their own group + `stop()` semantics.
- `lib/src/tools/checkpoint_tool.dart` — `checkpoint`/`rewind` tools:
  context hygiene for detours. `CheckpointRewindController` wraps
  `Agent.prepareNextTurn`, persists via host `CheckpointSessionSink`.
  Lifecycle (issue #286): a checkpoint is scoped to its detour — when the
  next `checkpoint` call finds it stale (a user turn arrived inside the
  detour, or the anchored span was rebuilt away by reload/compaction), it
  is auto-closed with a note + `checkpoint_auto_closed` session record
  instead of refusing; `rewind` semantics are unchanged.
- `lib/src/compaction/branch_summarization.dart` — `generateBranchSummary` +
  `navigateSessionTree` (use instead of `Session.moveTo` for tree
  navigation); summary is a `branch_summary` record on the entered branch.
- `lib/src/agent/tool_pairing.dart` — context pair-integrity (issue #85):
  `validateToolPairing` checks the wire-equivalent message sequence (orphan
  results, unanswered calls, duplicate ids, displaced results after
  same-role merges); `repairToolPairing` fixes the outbound payload only
  (drop orphan + note, synthesize interrupted results, hoist steering text
  after results, uniquify duplicate ids symmetrically on call+result).
  `agent_loop.dart` repairs before every request and retries once on a
  pairing-shaped provider 400 (`ToolPairingRepairEvent` is the audit
  trail); `_finishStreamed` stamps per-run position-counter ids
  session-unique; `auto_compactor.dart`'s `_localTrimFallback` routes the
  kept region through the same repairer.
- `lib/src/agent/image_registry.dart` — session image registry (issue
  #171): unique images ride a provider request exactly once; every other
  occurrence becomes a `[Image N]` text ref. `rewriteHistoryImages`
  rewrites the OUTBOUND payload only (session JSONL byte-identical);
  carriers `[{text:"[Image N]"},{image}]` anchor before the first
  referencing user message or after the tool-result run (never inside
  call/result pairs); the current user message rides images in place
  (I3), each in-place image carrying its `[Image N]` label (issue #195
  F3 — the model can cite what it sees); the per-request cap
  (`images.maxPerRequest`, default 20) drops current-first-then-newest
  with a drop notice (never silent; the app logs drops via `AppLog`,
  issue #195 F4); dangling refs (compaction, cap) resolve to `(image no
  longer available)`, and once a renumbering boundary exists (compaction
  summary, structured marker, local-trim note) AUTHORED history
  citations degrade to that note too — after renumbering an `[Image N]`
  may name a different image, so silent rebinding is never allowed
  (issue #195 F2; generated refs/labels stay content-keyed and fresh).
  Stateless per-request rebuild — determinism, compaction eviction and
  resume come free. Kill switch `images.registry: false` → byte-for-byte
  legacy shape. `agent_loop.dart` applies it in `_buildRequestContext`
  after `transformContext`, before tool-pairing repair.
- `lib/src/trajectory/` — the trajectory ledger core (issue #10): finalized
  session records project into an immutable `TrajectorySnapshot` through
  `TrajectorySnapshotBuilder.append`/`applyEvent` — streamed agent events
  land as synthetic rows keyed `turn\0step` (`u\0turn` for prompts) and are
  replaced when the real record lands; revision grows per append. Record
  kinds (closed set, `TrajectoryCellKind`): system, user, context,
  compacted, message, tool, subtool — a subtool is a
  `TrajectoryToolRecord.parentCallId != null`, which only hosts build
  directly (the builder never nests). Derived state folds once per
  snapshot: `deriveTrajectoryLayout` (turns of Message/S…

While the loop runs, let me study the race more deeply. Key facts:

1. The E4 test sequence:
   - `runWireServe` launched (boot in progress). Port pre-bound via `bindLoopback(0)`.
   - Bad-token `WebSocket.connect(...?token=wrong)` — expected to throw. If the handler isn't attached yet, the request sits buffered (single-subscription stream semantics of HttpServer) until `httpListen` attaches. Then → 401 → client throws.
   - Good-token `connect()` retry helper → upgrade OK → `attach()` → hello → welcome.

2. Where can "welcome never arrives in 10s" happen?

Let me think HARD about the buffering question. In Dart, `HttpServer.bind()` — after bind, the server starts accepting connections IMMEDIATELY (the accept loop is wired at bind time in the C++/event code). HTTP requests that arrive before a listen handler is attached are... Actually I recall dart:io's HttpServer is a `Stream<HttpRequest>`. Before `listen` is called, events (requests) arriving on a single-subscription stream are BUFFERED. Yes — HttpServer detaches into _HttpServer which implements Stream; incoming requests are added to the stream's internal buffer until a subscriber attaches. I'm fairly confident requests buffer rather than being dropped.

BUT — there's a subtlety: WebSocket CONNECT handshake requires the client to send the upgrade request AND wait. Client waits → fine, server responds when handler attaches.

OK here's another race candidate I should examine — **the bad-token client's socket half-close racing the server's request routing**. When the WS client gets the 401, dart:io throws `WebSocketException: Connection to 'ws://...' was not upgraded to websocket`. The client socket closes. Server: `await request.response.close()` completes. No server-side damage.

Hmm, so let me think about what ELSE could delay `welcome` by >10s in CI.

**Critical insight candidate:** `attach()` sets `_attaching = true` and listens to `decodeNdjson(server, ws.cast<Object>(), send)`. `decodeNdjson` is `messages.map(...).where(...)`. `attach` does `frames.listen(...)`. Now — WHEN does the server process the client's hello? The client sends hello AFTER `WebSocket.connect` resolves on the client side. Server side: `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade(request)` resolved → `attach` called → listen. Both sides' deliveries should proceed.

**What if `attach` never got called because the handler was still awaiting the FIRST (bad-token) request?** No — handlers run per-request independently; `http.forEach` invokes the handler for each request without waiting for the previous handler (forEach awaits the callback though! `http.forEach` — that's `Stream.forEach`, which WAITS for the async callback to complete before processing the NEXT stream event!). 

WAIT. THIS IS IT. `http.forEach((request) async {...})` — `Stream.forEach` processes events SEQUENTIALLY: it awaits the callback for each event before delivering the next. So if the bad-token request's handler is still awaiting something, the good-token request's handler START is BLOCKED.

But the bad-token handler completes quickly (401 + close). Unless... the buffered request ordering. Hmm, still fast.

blocks.text:
Same signature: `TimeoutException` at 538:21 — `ws.first` never completed within 10s.

Now let me think about the mechanics precisely, because I need a fix that addresses the root cause.

Test code path:

```dart
final served = cli.runWireServe(
  serve: (server) => httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token'),
  onDiagnostic: (line) => stderr.writeln(line),
);
// Wrong token: [REDACTED:Sensitive Value] is refused (HTTP 401)
await expectLater(
  WebSocket.connect('ws://127.0.0.1:${http.port}?token=wrong').then<void>((_) {}),
  throwsA(anything),
).timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));
// The right token works
final ws = await connect(http.port, token: '[REDACTED:Sensitive Value]');
ws.add(jsonEncode({...hello...}));
final first = await ws.first.timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));  // ← 538
```

Server path: `runWireServe` boots (async — `await _wireServeBoot(pumpSub)`) then calls `serve(server)` → `httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token')` → `http.forEach(handler)`.

Timeline analysis with `HttpServer` buffering:

1. `bindLoopback(0)` — server bound, TCP accepting (OS backlog + dart accept loop). Handler NOT attached yet.
2. Bad-token client connects. TCP accepted by dart (HttpServer accepts sockets immediately on bind — the socket is accepted and the request is parsed; the HttpRequest is added to the server stream's buffer since nobody listens yet).
3. Boot finishes (some ms). `serve` closure runs → `httpListen` → `http.forEach` attaches listener → buffered bad-token request delivered → 401 → client throws → expectLater passes.
4. Good-token connect attempt #1: if boot is done, upgrade proceeds... 

Wait — the retry helper is only needed if the server socket REFUSES. With pre-bind, connection always succeeds at TCP level. So attempt #1 awaits the handshake response — which comes once the handler processes the request. All sequential. The upgrade should succeed, `attach` runs, hello → welcome.

So how can `ws.first` hang for 10s with NO frame?

**Critical: `http.forEach` processes requests SEQUENTIALLY.** `Stream.forEach` waits for the async callback per event. So:

- Request A (bad token): handler starts. `tokenOk` fails → `response.statusCode = 401; await response.close()`. Quick. Done.
- Request B (good token): handler: tokenOk passes → `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade(request)` → ws → `attach(...)` → returns done.future (held until detach).

Hmm wait — `forEach` awaits the callback... The callback for request B awaits `server.attach(...).whenComplete(ws.close)` — i.e., the WHOLE client session. That means `http.forEach` stays pending until the client detaches. Fine — `listenDone` just hangs until shutdown; the serve closure races it with `shutdown.future`.

OK so sequencing-wise B's handler only STARTS after A's handler COMPLETES. If A's handler hangs (e.g., `await request.response.close()` never completes), B never gets processed → B's client handshake never gets a response → `connect()` helper: attempt #1's `WebSocket.connect` hangs forever (NOT an exception — so no retry, no fail) → `await connect(...)` at line 530 would hang — but the failure was at line 538, meaning `connect()` RETURNED. So the upgrade DID complete for B. Attach DID run (or did it?).

Wait — `connect()` returning means `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade` completed on the server (that's what produces the 101 response the client awaits). And `attach` is called immediately after the upgrade in the same handler. So `attach()` was called: either it took the `_shutDown` path, the `already_attached` path, or the normal path.

- `already_attached` path: sends an error FRAME → client would receive it → `ws.first` completes with `already_attached` → assertion fails (not timeout). NOT our case (we have a pure timeout).
- `_shutDown` path: sends `shutting_down` frame → same as above. NOT our case.
- Normal path: `_attaching = true`, `frames.listen(...)` on `decodeNdjson(server, ws.cast<Object>(), send)`.

In the normal path, the welcome is sent only when the client's HELLO is decoded and delivered to `_onClientFrame`. The client DID `ws.add(hello)` right after connect. For no frame to come back within 10s:

**Possibility 1: The server-side WS never delivered the hello to the decodeNdjson stream.** Why? The `ws.cast<Object>()` + `map` + `where` — `attach` listens immediately after `upgrade` returns. Events can't be lost (single-subscription stream buffers). Hmm.

**Possibility 2: The server never got the hello because the CLIENT never sent it.** The client's `ws.add(...)` right after `WebSocket.connect` resolves... `WebSocket.add` queues the frame for delivery. No reason to stall.

**Possibility 3: THE WELCOME WAS SENT BUT INTO THE WRONG SINK / the client was connected to a DIFFERENT (stale) server.** Hmm! Wait — in-process, each test boots its own AgentCli and binds its own port. E4's port is fresh (`bindLoopback(0)`).

**Possibility 4: The event loop was blocked.** Something in the process hogging the single thread >10s. CI log timeline: E4 started ~00:36:01.14 (right after IT-3 at 00:36:01.138). Failed 00:36:11.189. If the isolate's event loop were blocked, the `.timeout` wouldn't fire either... it did fire exactly at 10s. So the event loop was alive. The dart test runner runs tests concurrently (--concurrency=4 within this suite — other tests running simultaneously). The event loop being alive means timers fire. So the server's async machinery had CPU — but the welcome still didn't arrive.

**Possibility 5 — THE BIG ONE: the `connect()` helper stacked connections.** Here's the thing I dismissed: WHEN does `WebSocket.connect` throw? On connection-refused or bad response. The port is pre-bound, so connect at TCP always succeeds... BUT what about a request sent BEFORE the handler attached? The client awaits the response — buffered server-side. Not an exception.

BUT WAIT — look at the FIRST E4 phase (bad-token expectLater): `WebSocket.connect(...).then<void>((_) {})` — expected to throw. What if the server responds 101?! No — tokenOk fails for 'wrong'... `tokenOk(request, 'sekrit-token')` with `?token=wrong` → false → 401. OK.

Hmm, hold on. What if the bad-token request's 401 response races the client such that `WebSocket.connect` throws NOT because of 401 but because the socket closed? Either way it throws → expectLater passes.

**Possibility 6: `_attaching` got STUCK true → good-token attach → `already_attached` → but the frame WAS sent... to the client...** — we ruled that out because the client would receive the error frame and `ws.first` would complete (test would fail on the expect, not timeout). UNLESS the error frame send FAILS or the frame never reaches the client because... hmm, `_sendSafely`? Let me look at `_sendSafely` — maybe it swallows errors. But the socket is a fresh upgrade; sending works.

Hmm wait, actually let me re-examine: is it possible that `connect()` retried MULTIPLE times, with earlier attempts creating GHOST attaches? For an attempt to fail with an exception, the handshake must fail. With a pre-bound port and the handler attached, the handshake only fails on bad token. With the handler NOT yet attached, the request buffers → no exception → hangs until handler attaches.

**Now the CRITICAL scenario: what if `WebSocket.connect` (dart:io client) FAILS when the response's connection is closed by the server before the upgrade completes?** — i.e., E4 phase 1: the bad-token client. When `response.close()` runs, the client sees the 401 and throws `WebSocketException`. Standard.

OK here's another thought — **the `_attaching` flag stuck-true via a PREVIOUS attach in the SAME server instance**: E4 is the only attach in its own `server` instance (fresh per `runWireServe`). Prior tests don't share it. So no.

Hmm, let me look at Possibility 4 variant: **the boot path (`_wireServeBoot`) has an await that blocks until something external happens** — e.g., `_claimSessionLeaseHeadless`, `_initializeSession`, `acquirePowerAssertions`, `_warmModelCacheQuietly`, `_maybeAutoCompact`, `_subagentManager.rehydrate()`, `AgentCliTools(this).rebuildToolAvailability()`, `_startInboxWatcher()`... messages.preview: Let me examine the send path and the protocol acceptHello, plus check how the client-side `ws.first` interacts:

blocks.text:
Same signature: `TimeoutException` at 538:21 — `ws.first` never completed within 10s.

Now let me think about the mechanics precisely, because I need a fix that addresses the root cause.

Test code path:

```dart
final served = cli.runWireServe(
  serve: (server) => httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token'),
  onDiagnostic: (line) => stderr.writeln(line),
);
// Wrong token: [REDACTED:Sensitive Value] is refused (HTTP 401)
await expectLater(
  WebSocket.connect('ws://127.0.0.1:${http.port}?token=wrong').then<void>((_) {}),
  throwsA(anything),
).timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));
// The right token works
final ws = await connect(http.port, token: '[REDACTED:Sensitive Value]');
ws.add(jsonEncode({...hello...}));
final first = await ws.first.timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));  // ← 538
```

Server path: `runWireServe` boots (async — `await _wireServeBoot(pumpSub)`) then calls `serve(server)` → `httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token')` → `http.forEach(handler)`.

Timeline analysis with `HttpServer` buffering:

1. `bindLoopback(0)` — server bound, TCP accepting (OS backlog + dart accept loop). Handler NOT attached yet.
2. Bad-token client connects. TCP accepted by dart (HttpServer accepts sockets immediately on bind — the socket is accepted and the request is parsed; the HttpRequest is added to the server stream's buffer since nobody listens yet).
3. Boot finishes (some ms). `serve` closure runs → `httpListen` → `http.forEach` attaches listener → buffered bad-token request delivered → 401 → client throws → expectLater passes.
4. Good-token connect attempt #1: if boot is done, upgrade proceeds... 

Wait — the retry helper is only needed if the server socket REFUSES. With pre-bind, connection always succeeds at TCP level. So attempt #1 awaits the handshake response — which comes once the handler processes the request. All sequential. The upgrade should succeed, `attach` runs, hello → welcome.

So how can `ws.first` hang for 10s with NO frame?

**Critical: `http.forEach` processes requests SEQUENTIALLY.** `Stream.forEach` waits for the async callback per event. So:

- Request A (bad token): handler starts. `tokenOk` fails → `response.statusCode = 401; await response.close()`. Quick. Done.
- Request B (good token): handler: tokenOk passes → `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade(request)` → ws → `attach(...)` → returns done.future (held until detach).

Hmm wait — `forEach` awaits the callback... The callback for request B awaits `server.attach(...).whenComplete(ws.close)` — i.e., the WHOLE client session. That means `http.forEach` stays pending until the client detaches. Fine — `listenDone` just hangs until shutdown; the serve closure races it with `shutdown.future`.

OK so sequencing-wise B's handler only STARTS after A's handler COMPLETES. If A's handler hangs (e.g., `await request.response.close()` never completes), B never gets processed → B's client handshake never gets a response → `connect()` helper: attempt #1's `WebSocket.connect` hangs forever (NOT an exception — so no retry, no fail) → `await connect(...)` at line 530 would hang — but the failure was at line 538, meaning `connect()` RETURNED. So the upgrade DID complete for B. Attach DID run (or did it?).

Wait — `connect()` returning means `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade` completed on the server (that's what produces the 101 response the client awaits). And `attach` is called immediately after the upgrade in the same handler. So `attach()` was called: either it took the `_shutDown` path, the `already_attached` path, or the normal path.

- `already_attached` path: sends an error FRAME → client would receive it → `ws.first` completes with `already_attached` → assertion fails (not timeout). NOT our case (we have a pure timeout).
- `_shutDown` path: sends `shutting_down` frame → same as above. NOT our case.
- Normal path: `_attaching = true`, `frames.listen(...)` on `decodeNdjson(server, ws.cast<Object>(), send)`.

In the normal path, the welcome is sent only when the client's HELLO is decoded and delivered to `_onClientFrame`. The client DID `ws.add(hello)` right after connect. For no frame to come back within 10s:

**Possibility 1: The server-side WS never delivered the hello to the decodeNdjson stream.** Why? The `ws.cast<Object>()` + `map` + `where` — `attach` listens immediately after `upgrade` returns. Events can't be lost (single-subscription stream buffers). Hmm.

**Possibility 2: The server never got the hello because the CLIENT never sent it.** The client's `ws.add(...)` right after `WebSocket.connect` resolves... `WebSocket.add` queues the frame for delivery. No reason to stall.

**Possibility 3: THE WELCOME WAS SENT BUT INTO THE WRONG SINK / the client was connected to a DIFFERENT (stale) server.** Hmm! Wait — in-process, each test boots its own AgentCli and binds its own port. E4's port is fresh (`bindLoopback(0)`).

**Possibility 4: The event loop was blocked.** Something in the process hogging the single thread >10s. CI log timeline: E4 started ~00:36:01.14 (right after IT-3 at 00:36:01.138). Failed 00:36:11.189. If the isolate's event loop were blocked, the `.timeout` wouldn't fire either... it did fire exactly at 10s. So the event loop was alive. The dart test runner runs tests concurrently (--concurrency=4 within this suite — other tests running simultaneously). The event loop being alive means timers fire. So the server's async machinery had CPU — but the welcome still didn't arrive.

**Possibility 5 — THE BIG ONE: the `connect()` helper stacked connections.** Here's the thing I dismissed: WHEN does `WebSocket.connect` throw? On connection-refused or bad response. The port is pre-bound, so connect at TCP always succeeds... BUT what about a request sent BEFORE the handler attached? The client awaits the response — buffered server-side. Not an exception.

BUT WAIT — look at the FIRST E4 phase (bad-token expectLater): `WebSocket.connect(...).then<void>((_) {})` — expected to throw. What if the server responds 101?! No — tokenOk fails for 'wrong'... `tokenOk(request, 'sekrit-token')` with `?token=wrong` → false → 401. OK.

Hmm, hold on. What if the bad-token request's 401 response races the client such that `WebSocket.connect` throws NOT because of 401 but because the socket closed? Either way it throws → expectLater passes.

**Possibility 6: `_attaching` got STUCK true → good-token attach → `already_attached` → but the frame WAS sent... to the client...** — we ruled that out because the client would receive the error frame and `ws.first` would complete (test would fail on the expect, not timeout). 2. Where can "welcome never arrives in 10s" happen?

Let me think HARD about the buffering question. In Dart, `HttpServer.bind()` — after bind, the server starts accepting connections IMMEDIATELY (the accept loop is wired at bind time in the C++/event code). HTTP requests that arrive before a listen handler is attached are... Actually I recall dart:io's HttpServer is a `Stream<HttpRequest>`. Before `listen` is called, events (requests) arriving on a single-subscription stream are BUFFERED. Yes — HttpServer detaches into _HttpServer which implements Stream; incoming requests are added to the stream's internal buffer until a subscriber attaches. I'm fairly confident requests buffer rather than being dropped.

BUT — there's a subtlety: WebSocket CONNECT handshake requires the client to send the upgrade request AND wait. Client waits → fine, server responds when handler attaches.

OK here's another race candidate I should examine — **the bad-token client's socket half-close racing the server's request routing**. When the WS client gets the 401, dart:io throws `WebSocketException: Connection to 'ws://...' was not upgraded to websocket`. The client socket closes. Server: `await request.response.close()` completes. No server-side damage.

Hmm, so let me think about what ELSE could delay `welcome` by >10s in CI.

**Critical insight candidate:** `attach()` sets `_attaching = true` and listens to `decodeNdjson(server, ws.cast<Object>(), send)`. `decodeNdjson` is `messages.map(...).where(...)`. `attach` does `frames.listen(...)`. Now — WHEN does the server process the client's hello? The client sends hello AFTER `WebSocket.connect` resolves on the client side. Server side: `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade(request)` resolved → `attach` called → listen. Both sides' deliveries should proceed.

**What if `attach` never got called because the handler was still awaiting the FIRST (bad-token) request?** No — handlers run per-request independently; `http.forEach` invokes the handler for each request without waiting for the previous handler (forEach awaits the callback though! `http.forEach` — that's `Stream.forEach`, which WAITS for the async callback to complete before processing the NEXT stream event!).

But the bad-token handler completes quickly (401 + close). Unless... the buffered request ordering. Hmm, still fast.

messages.preview: Let me examine the send path and the protocol acceptHello, plus check how the client-side `ws.first` interacts:

blocks.text:
Same signature: `TimeoutException` at 538:21 — `ws.first` never completed within 10s.

Now let me think about the mechanics precisely, because I need a fix that addresses the root cause.

Test code path:

```dart
final served = cli.runWireServe(
  serve: (server) => httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token'),
  onDiagnostic: (line) => stderr.writeln(line),
);
// Wrong token: [REDACTED:Sensitive Value] is refused (HTTP 401)
await expectLater(
  WebSocket.connect('ws://127.0.0.1:${http.port}?token=wrong').then<void>((_) {}),
  throwsA(anything),
).timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));
// The right token works
final ws = await connect(http.port, token: '[REDACTED:Sensitive Value]');
ws.add(jsonEncode({...hello...}));
final first = await ws.first.timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));  // ← 538
```

Server path: `runWireServe` boots (async — `await _wireServeBoot(pumpSub)`) then calls `serve(server)` → `httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token')` → `http.forEach(handler)`.

Timeline analysis with `HttpServer` buffering:

1. `bindLoopback(0)` — server bound, TCP accepting (OS backlog + dart accept loop). Handler NOT attached yet.
2. Bad-token client connects. TCP accepted by dart (HttpServer accepts sockets immediately on bind — the socket is accepted and the request is parsed; the HttpRequest is added to the server stream's buffer since nobody listens yet).
3. Boot finishes (some ms). `serve` closure runs → `httpListen` → `http.forEach` attaches listener → buffered bad-token request delivered → 401 → client throws → expectLater passes.
4. Good-token connect attempt #1: if boot is done, upgrade proceeds... 

Wait — the retry helper is only needed if the server socket REFUSES. With pre-bind, connection always succeeds at TCP level. So attempt #1 awaits the handshake response — which comes once the handler processes the request. All sequential. The upgrade should succeed, `attach` runs, hello → welcome.

So how can `ws.first` hang for 10s with NO frame?

**Critical: `http.forEach` processes requests SEQUENTIALLY.** `Stream.forEach` waits for the async callback per event. So:

- Request A (bad token): handler starts. `tokenOk` fails → `response.statusCode = 401; await response.close()`. Quick. Done.
- Request B (good token): handler: tokenOk passes → `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade(request)` → ws → `attach(...)` → returns done.future (held until detach).

Hmm wait — `forEach` awaits the callback... The callback for request B awaits `server.attach(...).whenComplete(ws.close)` — i.e., the WHOLE client session. That means `http.forEach` stays pending until the client detaches. Fine — `listenDone` just hangs until shutdown; the serve closure races it with `shutdown.future`.

OK so sequencing-wise B's handler only STARTS after A's handler COMPLETES. If A's handler hangs (e.g., `await request.response.close()` never completes), B never gets processed → B's client handshake never gets a response → `connect()` helper: attempt #1's `WebSocket.connect` hangs forever (NOT an exception — so no retry, no fail) → `await connect(...)` at line 530 would hang — but the failure was at line 538, meaning `connect()` RETURNED. So the upgrade DID complete for B. Attach DID run (or did it?).

Wait — `connect()` returning means `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade` completed on the server (that's what produces the 101 response the client awaits). And `attach` is called immediately after the upgrade in the same handler. So `attach()` was called: either it took the `_shutDown` path, the `already_attached` path, or the normal path.

- `already_attached` path: sends an error FRAME → client would receive it → `ws.first` completes with `already_attached` → assertion fails (not timeout). NOT our case (we have a pure timeout).
- `_shutDown` path: sends `shutting_down` frame → same as above. NOT our case.
- Normal path: `_attaching = true`, `frames.listen(...)` on `decodeNdjson(server, ws.cast<Object>(), send)`.

In the normal path, the welcome is sent only when the client's HELLO is decoded and delivered to `_onClientFrame`. The client DID `ws.add(hello)` right after connect. For no frame to come back within 10s:

**Possibility 1: The server-side WS never delivered the hello to the decodeNdjson stream.** Why? The `ws.cast<Object>()` + `map` + `where` — `attach` listens immediately after `upgrade` returns. Events can't be lost (single-subscription stream buffers). Hmm.

**Possibility 2: The server never got the hello because the CLIENT never sent it.** The client's `ws.add(...)` right after `WebSocket.connect` resolves... `WebSocket.add` queues the frame for delivery. No reason to stall.

**Possibility 3: THE WELCOME WAS SENT BUT INTO THE WRONG SINK / the client was connected to a DIFFERENT (stale) server.** Hmm! Wait — in-process, each test boots its own AgentCli and binds its own port. E4's port is fresh (`bindLoopback(0)`).

**Possibility 4: The event loop was blocked.** Something in the process hogging the single thread >10s. CI log timeline: E4 started ~00:36:01.14 (right after IT-3 at 00:36:01.138). Failed 00:36:11.189. If the isolate's event loop were blocked, the `.timeout` wouldn't fire either... it did fire exactly at 10s. So the event loop was alive. The dart test runner runs tests concurrently (--concurrency=4 within this suite — other tests running simultaneously). The event loop being alive means timers fire. So the server's async machinery had CPU — but the welcome still didn't arrive.

**Possibility 5 — THE BIG ONE: the `connect()` helper stacked connections.** Here's the thing I dismissed: WHEN does `WebSocket.connect` throw? On connection-refused or bad response. The port is pre-bound, so connect at TCP always succeeds... BUT what about a request sent BEFORE the handler attached? The client awaits the response — buffered server-side. Not an exception.

BUT WAIT — look at the FIRST E4 phase (bad-token expectLater): `WebSocket.connect(...).then<void>((_) {})` — expected to throw. What if the server responds 101?! No — tokenOk fails for 'wrong'... `tokenOk(request, 'sekrit-token')` with `?token=wrong` → false → 401. OK.

Hmm, hold on. What if the bad-token request's 401 response races the client such that `WebSocket.connect` throws NOT because of 401 but because the socket closed? Either way it throws → expectLater passes.

**Possibility 6: `_attaching` got STUCK true → good-token attach → `already_attached` → but the frame WAS sent... to the client...** — we ruled that out because the client would receive the error frame and `ws.first` would complete (test would fail on the expect, not timeout). UNLESS the error frame send FAILS or the frame never reaches the client because... hmm, `_sendSafely`? Let me look at `_sendSafely` — maybe it swallows errors. But the socket is a fresh upgrade; sending works.

Hmm wait, actually let me re-examine: is it possible that `connect()` retried MULTIPLE times, with earlier attempts creating GHOST attaches? messages.preview: Let me examine the send path and the protocol acceptHello, plus check how the client-side `ws.first` interacts:

blocks.text:
Same signature: `TimeoutException` at 538:21 — `ws.first` never completed within 10s.

Now let me think about the mechanics precisely, because I need a fix that addresses the root cause.

Test code path:

```dart
final served = cli.runWireServe(
  serve: (server) => httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token'),
  onDiagnostic: (line) => stderr.writeln(line),
);
// Wrong token: [REDACTED:Sensitive Value] is refused (HTTP 401)
await expectLater(
  WebSocket.connect('ws://127.0.0.1:${http.port}?token=wrong').then<void>((_) {}),
  throwsA(anything),
).timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));
// The right token works
final ws = await connect(http.port, token: '[REDACTED:Sensitive Value]');
ws.add(jsonEncode({...hello...}));
final first = await ws.first.timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));  // ← 538
```

Server path: `runWireServe` boots (async — `await _wireServeBoot(pumpSub)`) then calls `serve(server)` → `httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token')` → `http.forEach(handler)`.

Timeline analysis with `HttpServer` buffering:

1. `bindLoopback(0)` — server bound, TCP accepting (OS backlog + dart accept loop). Handler NOT attached yet.
2. Bad-token client connects. TCP accepted by dart (HttpServer accepts sockets immediately on bind — the socket is accepted and the request is parsed; the HttpRequest is added to the server stream's buffer since nobody listens yet).
3. Boot finishes (some ms). `serve` closure runs → `httpListen` → `http.forEach` attaches listener → buffered bad-token request delivered → 401 → client throws → expectLater passes.
4. Good-token connect attempt #1: if boot is done, upgrade proceeds... 

Wait — the retry helper is only needed if the server socket REFUSES. With pre-bind, connection always succeeds at TCP level. So attempt #1 awaits the handshake response — which comes once the handler processes the request. All sequential. The upgrade should succeed, `attach` runs, hello → welcome.

So how can `ws.first` hang for 10s with NO frame?

**Critical: `http.forEach` processes requests SEQUENTIALLY.** `Stream.forEach` waits for the async callback per event. So:

- Request A (bad token): handler starts. `tokenOk` fails → `response.statusCode = 401; await response.close()`. Quick. Done.
- Request B (good token): handler: tokenOk passes → `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade(request)` → ws → `attach(...)` → returns done.future (held until detach).

Hmm wait — `forEach` awaits the callback... The callback for request B awaits `server.attach(...).whenComplete(ws.close)` — i.e., the WHOLE client session. That means `http.forEach` stays pending until the client detaches. Fine — `listenDone` just hangs until shutdown; the serve closure races it with `shutdown.future`.

OK so sequencing-wise B's handler only STARTS after A's handler COMPLETES. If A's handler hangs (e.g., `await request.response.close()` never completes), B never gets processed → B's client handshake never gets a response → `connect()` helper: attempt #1's `WebSocket.connect` hangs forever (NOT an exception — so no retry, no fail) → `await connect(...)` at line 530 would hang — but the failure was at line 538, meaning `connect()` RETURNED. So the upgrade DID complete for B. Attach DID run (or did it?).

Wait — `connect()` returning means `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade` completed on the server (that's what produces the 101 response the client awaits). And `attach` is called immediately after the upgrade in the same handler. So `attach()` was called: either it took the `_shutDown` path, the `already_attached` path, or the normal path.

Before `listen` is called, events (requests) arriving on a single-subscription stream are BUFFERED. BUT — there's a subtlety: WebSocket CONNECT handshake requires the client to send the upgrade request AND wait. Client waits → fine, server responds when handler attaches.

messages.preview: Let me examine the send path and the protocol acceptHello, plus check how the client-side `ws.first` interacts:

blocks.text:
Same signature: `TimeoutException` at 538:21 — `ws.first` never completed within 10s.

Now let me think about the mechanics precisely, because I need a fix that addresses the root cause.

Test code path:

```dart
final served = cli.runWireServe(
  serve: (server) => httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token'),
  onDiagnostic: (line) => stderr.writeln(line),
);
// Wrong token: [REDACTED:Sensitive Value] is refused (HTTP 401)
await expectLater(
  WebSocket.connect('ws://127.0.0.1:${http.port}?token=wrong').then<void>((_) {}),
  throwsA(anything),
).timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));
// The right token works
final ws = await connect(http.port, token: '[REDACTED:Sensitive Value]');
ws.add(jsonEncode({...hello...}));
final first = await ws.first.timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));  // ← 538
```

Server path: `runWireServe` boots (async — `await _wireServeBoot(pumpSub)`) then calls `serve(server)` → `httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token')` → `http.forEach(handler)`.

Timeline analysis with `HttpServer` buffering:

1. `bindLoopback(0)` — server bound, TCP accepting (OS backlog + dart accept loop). Handler NOT attached yet.
2. Bad-token client connects. TCP accepted by dart (HttpServer accepts sockets immediately on bind — the socket is accepted and the request is parsed; the HttpRequest is added to the server stream's buffer since nobody listens yet).
3. Boot finishes (some ms). `serve` closure runs → `httpListen` → `http.forEach` attaches listener → buffered bad-token request delivered → 401 → client throws → expectLater passes.
4. Good-token connect attempt #1: if boot is done, upgrade proceeds... 

Wait — the retry helper is only needed if the server socket REFUSES. With pre-bind, connection always succeeds at TCP level. So attempt #1 awaits the handshake response — which comes once the handler processes the request. All sequential. The upgrade should succeed, `attach` runs, hello → welcome.

So how can `ws.first` hang for 10s with NO frame?

**Critical: `http.forEach` processes requests SEQUENTIALLY.** `Stream.forEach` waits for the async callback per event. So:

- Request A (bad token): handler starts. `tokenOk` fails → `response.statusCode = 401; await response.close()`. Quick. Done.
- Request B (good token): handler: tokenOk passes → `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade(request)` → ws → `attach(...)` → returns done.future (held until detach).

Hmm wait — `forEach` awaits the callback... The callback for request B awaits `server.attach(...).whenComplete(ws.close)` — i.e., the WHOLE client session. That means `http.forEach` stays pending until the client detaches. Fine — `listenDone` just hangs until shutdown; the serve closure races it with `shutdown.future`.

OK so sequencing-wise B's handler only STARTS after A's handler COMPLETES. If A's handler hangs (e.g., `await request.response.close()` never completes), B never gets processed → B's client handshake never gets a response → `connect()` helper: attempt #1's `WebSocket.connect` hangs forever (NOT an exception — so no retry, no fail) → `await connect(...)` at line 530 would hang — but the failure was at line 538, meaning `connect()` RETURNED. So the upgrade DID complete for B. Attach DID run (or did it?).

Wait — `connect()` returning means `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade` completed on the server (that's what produces the 101 response the client awaits). Now let me understand `WireServer.attach` — the single-attach gate in `lib/src/wire/wire_serve.dart`. The welcome frame is sent upon attach (or upon hello?). The test: client connects, sends `hello`, then expects `welcome` as the FIRST frame (`ws.first`).

The bad-token `WebSocket.connect('ws://127.0.0.1:port?token=wrong')`:
- The HTTP server is already bound (bindLoopback happened before `runWireServe`).
- If the request arrives BEFORE `http.forEach` is attached (serve closure not yet run — boot takes a moment), the HttpRequest is... in Dart, `HttpServer` is a `Stream<HttpRequest>`; events arriving before `listen` are buffered by the stream (single-subscription streams buffer events). So the request waits.
- When `httpListen` attaches, the buffered request is delivered: it's an upgrade request with a bad token → 401 → `request.response.close()`. The WS client sees 401 → throws `WebSocketException` (or HttpException). Good.

Then the good-token connect: retry helper → connects → upgrade OK → `server.attach(...)` called with the new frame stream.

Now the question: why would `welcome` not arrive for 10s? Let me read `wire_serve.dart` — the pure core — especially `attach` and what triggers the `welcome` frame. It's probably: attach completes, then waits for the client's `hello`, then replies `welcome`. The single-attach gate: if `already_attached`, send an error frame instead.

Hmm wait — what if the bad-token WebSocket client's TCP connection... no.

Actually — here's another thought: THE RETRY HELPER. Consider this interleaving:

1. Bad-token connect attempt starts BEFORE the server handler attached. The request is buffered in the HttpServer stream.
2. Retry-helper good-token connect ALSO starts (only after bad-token expectLater completes — no, it's sequential: bad-token expectLater completes only when WebSocket.connect throws, which happens only after the 401 response arrives, which happens only after httpListen attached and processed the request). In Dart, `HttpServer.bind()` — after bind, the server starts accepting connections IMMEDIATELY (the accept loop is wired at bind time in the C++/event code). HTTP requests that arrive before a listen handler is attached are... Actually I recall dart:io's HttpServer is a `Stream<HttpRequest>`. Before `listen` is called, events (requests) arriving on a single-subscription stream are BUFFERED. Yes — HttpServer detaches into _HttpServer which implements Stream; incoming requests are added to the stream's internal buffer until a subscriber attaches. I'm fairly confident requests buffer rather than being dropped.

BUT — there's a subtlety: WebSocket CONNECT handshake requires the client to send the upgrade request AND wait. Client waits → fine, server responds when handler attaches.

OK here's another race candidate I should examine — **the bad-token client's socket half-close racing the server's request routing**. When the WS client gets the 401, dart:io throws `WebSocketException: Connection to 'ws://...' was not upgraded to websocket`. The client socket closes. messages.preview: Let me examine the send path and the protocol acceptHello, plus check how the client-side `ws.first` interacts:

blocks.text:
Same signature: `TimeoutException` at 538:21 — `ws.first` never completed within 10s.

Now let me think about the mechanics precisely, because I need a fix that addresses the root cause.

Test code path:

```dart
final served = cli.runWireServe(
  serve: (server) => httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token'),
  onDiagnostic: (line) => stderr.writeln(line),
);
// Wrong token: [REDACTED:Sensitive Value] is refused (HTTP 401)
await expectLater(
  WebSocket.connect('ws://127.0.0.1:${http.port}?token=wrong').then<void>((_) {}),
  throwsA(anything),
).timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));
// The right token works
final ws = await connect(http.port, token: '[REDACTED:Sensitive Value]');
ws.add(jsonEncode({...hello...}));
final first = await ws.first.timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));  // ← 538
```

Server path: `runWireServe` boots (async — `await _wireServeBoot(pumpSub)`) then calls `serve(server)` → `httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token')` → `http.forEach(handler)`.

Timeline analysis with `HttpServer` buffering:

1. `bindLoopback(0)` — server bound, TCP accepting (OS backlog + dart accept loop). Handler NOT attached yet.
2. Bad-token client connects. TCP accepted by dart (HttpServer accepts sockets immediately on bind — the socket is accepted and the request is parsed; the HttpRequest is added to the server stream's buffer since nobody listens yet).
3. Boot finishes (some ms). `serve` closure runs → `httpListen` → `http.forEach` attaches listener → buffered bad-token request delivered → 401 → client throws → expectLater passes.
4. Good-token connect attempt #1: if boot is done, upgrade proceeds... 

Wait — the retry helper is only needed if the server socket REFUSES. With pre-bind, connection always succeeds at TCP level. So attempt #1 awaits the handshake response — which comes once the handler processes the request. All sequential. The upgrade should succeed, `attach` runs, hello → welcome.

So how can `ws.first` hang for 10s with NO frame?

**Critical: `http.forEach` processes requests SEQUENTIALLY.** `Stream.forEach` waits for the async callback per event. So:

- Request A (bad token): handler starts. `tokenOk` fails → `response.statusCode = 401; await response.close()`. Quick. Done.
- Request B (good token): handler: tokenOk passes → `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade(request)` → ws → `attach(...)` → returns done.future (held until detach).

Hmm wait — `forEach` awaits the callback... The callback for request B awaits `server.attach(...).whenComplete(ws.close)` — i.e., the WHOLE client session. That means `http.forEach` stays pending until the client detaches. Fine — `listenDone` just hangs until shutdown; the serve closure races it with `shutdown.future`.

OK so sequencing-wise B's handler only STARTS after A's handler COMPLETES. If A's handler hangs (e.g., `await request.response.close()` never completes), B never gets processed → B's client handshake never gets a response → `connect()` helper: attempt #1's `WebSocket.connect` hangs forever (NOT an exception — so no retry, no fail) → `await connect(...)` at line 530 would hang — but the failure was at line 538, meaning `connect()` RETURNED. So the upgrade DID complete for B. Attach DID run (or did it?).

Wait — `connect()` returning means `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade` completed on the server (that's what produces the 101 response the client awaits). And `attach` is called immediately after the upgrade in the same handler. So `attach()` was called: either it took the `_shutDown` path, the `already_attached` path, or the normal path.

- `already_attached` path: sends an error FRAME → client would receive it → `ws.first` completes with `already_attached` → assertion fails (not timeout). NOT our case (we have a pure timeout).
- `_shutDown` path: sends `shutting_down` frame → same as above. NOT our case.
- Normal path: `_attaching = true`, `frames.listen(...)` on `decodeNdjson(server, ws.cast<Object>(), send)`.

In the normal path, the welcome is sent only when the client's HELLO is decoded and delivered to `_onClientFrame`. The client DID `ws.add(hello)` right after connect. For no frame to come back within 10s:

**Possibility 1: The server-side WS never delivered the hello to the decodeNdjson stream.** Why? The `ws.cast<Object>()` + `map` + `where` — `attach` listens immediately after `upgrade` returns. Events can't be lost (single-subscription stream buffers). Hmm.

**Possibility 2: The server never got the hello because the CLIENT never sent it.** The client's `ws.add(...)` right after `WebSocket.connect` resolves... `WebSocket.add` queues the frame for delivery. No reason to stall.

**Possibility 3: THE WELCOME WAS SENT BUT INTO THE WRONG SINK / the client was connected to a DIFFERENT (stale) server.** Hmm! Wait — in-process, each test boots its own AgentCli and binds its own port. E4's port is fresh (`bindLoopback(0)`).

messages.preview: Let me examine the send path and the protocol acceptHello, plus check how the client-side `ws.first` interacts:

blocks.text:
Same signature: `TimeoutException` at 538:21 — `ws.first` never completed within 10s.

Now let me think about the mechanics precisely, because I need a fix that addresses the root cause.

Test code path:

```dart
final served = cli.runWireServe(
  serve: (server) => httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token'),
  onDiagnostic: (line) => stderr.writeln(line),
);
// Wrong token: [REDACTED:Sensitive Value] is refused (HTTP 401)
await expectLater(
  WebSocket.connect('ws://127.0.0.1:${http.port}?token=wrong').then<void>((_) {}),
  throwsA(anything),
).timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));
// The right token works
final ws = await connect(http.port, token: '[REDACTED:Sensitive Value]');
ws.add(jsonEncode({...hello...}));
final first = await ws.first.timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));  // ← 538
```

Server path: `runWireServe` boots (async — `await _wireServeBoot(pumpSub)`) then calls `serve(server)` → `httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token')` → `http.forEach(handler)`.

Timeline analysis with `HttpServer` buffering:

1. `bindLoopback(0)` — server bound, TCP accepting (OS backlog + dart accept loop). Handler NOT attached yet.
2. Bad-token client connects. TCP accepted by dart (HttpServer accepts sockets immediately on bind — the socket is accepted and the request is parsed; the HttpRequest is added to the server stream's buffer since nobody listens yet).
3. Boot finishes (some ms). `serve` closure runs → `httpListen` → `http.forEach` attaches listener → buffered bad-token request delivered → 401 → client throws → expectLater passes.
4. Good-token connect attempt #1: if boot is done, upgrade proceeds... 

Wait — the retry helper is only needed if the server socket REFUSES. With pre-bind, connection always succeeds at TCP level. So attempt #1 awaits the handshake response — which comes once the handler processes the request. All sequential. The upgrade should succeed, `attach` runs, hello → welcome.

So how can `ws.first` hang for 10s with NO frame?

**Critical: `http.forEach` processes requests SEQUENTIALLY.** `Stream.forEach` waits for the async callback per event. So:

- Request A (bad token): handler starts. `tokenOk` fails → `response.statusCode = 401; await response.close()`. Quick. Done.
- Request B (good token): handler: tokenOk passes → `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade(request)` → ws → `attach(...)` → returns done.future (held until detach).

Hmm wait — `forEach` awaits the callback... The callback for request B awaits `server.attach(...).whenComplete(ws.close)` — i.e., the WHOLE client session. That means `http.forEach` stays pending until the client detaches. Fine — `listenDone` just hangs until shutdown; the serve closure races it with `shutdown.future`.

OK so sequencing-wise B's handler only STARTS after A's handler COMPLETES. If A's handler hangs (e.g., `await request.response.close()` never completes), B never gets processed → B's client handshake never gets a response → `connect()` helper: attempt #1's `WebSocket.connect` hangs forever (NOT an exception — so no retry, no fail) → `await connect(...)` at line 530 would hang — but the failure was at line 538, meaning `connect()` RETURNED. So the upgrade DID complete for B. Attach DID run (or did it?).

Wait — `connect()` returning means `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade` completed on the server (that's what produces the 101 response the client awaits). And `attach` is called immediately after the upgrade in the same handler. So `attach()` was called: either it took the `_shutDown` path, the `already_attached` path, or the normal path.

- `already_attached` path: sends an error FRAME → client would receive it → `ws.first` completes with `already_attached` → assertion fails (not timeout). NOT our case (we have a pure timeout).
- `_shutDown` path: sends `shutting_down` frame → same as above. NOT our case.
- Normal path: `_attaching = true`, `frames.listen(...)` on `decodeNdjson(server, ws.cast<Object>(), send)`.

In the normal path, the welcome is sent only when the client's HELLO is decoded and delivered to `_onClientFrame`. The client DID `ws.add(hello)` right after connect. For no frame to come back within 10s:

**Possibility 1: The server-side WS never delivered the hello to the decodeNdjson stream.** Why? The `ws.cast<Object>()` + `map` + `where` — `attach` listens immediately after `upgrade` returns. Events can't be lost (single-subscription stream buffers). Hmm.

**Possibility 2: The server never got the hello because the CLIENT never sent it.** The client's `ws.add(...)` right after `WebSocket.connect` resolves... `WebSocket.add` queues the frame for delivery. No reason to stall.

**Possibility 3: THE WELCOME WAS SENT BUT INTO THE WRONG SINK / the client was connected to a DIFFERENT (stale) server.** Hmm! Wait — in-process, each test boots its own AgentCli and binds its own port. E4's port is fresh (`bindLoopback(0)`).

**Possibility 4: The event loop was blocked.** Something in the process hogging the single thread >10s. CI log timeline: E4 started ~00:36:01.14 (right after IT-3 at 00:36:01.138). Failed 00:36:11.189. If the isolate's event loop were blocked, the `.timeout` wouldn't fire either... it did fire exactly at 10s. So the event loop was alive. The dart test runner runs tests concurrently (--concurrency=4 within this suite — other tests running simultaneously). The event loop being alive means timers fire. Now I see the attach flow:

1. `attach(frames, send)` is called per WS connection from `httpListen`.
2. Guard: `if (_client != null || _attaching)` → send `already_attached` and return.
3. Otherwise `_attaching = true`, listen on frames. First frame must be `hello` → `welcome` sent, `_client = send`.

Race analysis for the E4 test:

The bad-token request: it gets a 401 in `httpListen` (tokenOk fails) → `request.response.close()`. The WS client throws. `expectLater` passes.

Then good-token connect via helper → `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade` succeeds → `server.attach(...)` called → `_attaching = true` → subscription set up. Client sends hello → `_onClientFrame` → acceptHello → welcome. This all seems fine.

So where's the flake? Let me think about the bad-token request arriving BEFORE `httpListen` attaches. In Dart, `HttpServer` is a single-subscription stream. Requests that arrive before `listen` — I need to check Dart's behavior: does `HttpServer` buffer them? If the server receives a request before the listener attaches, the connection is accepted at the OS level and the HttpRequest object is created, but the stream events... `HttpServer` implements `Stream<HttpRequest>`; events emitted before listen are buffered (standard single-subscription stream semantics). So they get delivered when `forEach` (which calls listen) attaches. OK.

Now the retry helper: it retries when `WebSocket.connect` THROWS. With the port pre-bound, does `WebSocket.connect` ever throw before the handler attaches? The TCP connection is accepted by the OS (backlog), and Dart's HttpServer accepts the socket into its internal connection pool even before listen (I believe connections are accepted immediately upon bind; requests are only delivered via the stream once listened... hmm, actually I'm not 100% sure whether Dart accepts sockets before listen — the accept loop is wired in `bind`).

Regardless: the client's WS handshake request gets a response only after the handler processes it. Until then, `WebSocket.connect` awaits. No throw → no retry. So stacking only if requests FAIL fast. Connection-refused can't happen (port bound). So the "stacking" hypothesis is questionable...

UNLESS — the 401 response. Look carefully at `httpListen`'s bad-token branch:

```dart
if (!tokenOk(request, token)) {
  request.response.statusCode = HttpStatus.unauthorized;
  await request.response.close();
  return;
}
```

When the client `WebSocket.connect` receives the 401, dart:io's WebSocketTransport... the client throws `WebSocketException('Connection to ... was not upgraded to websocket')` — and importantly, the client may leave the socket in a weird state, but the server side already closed the response.

Hmm OK. But here's another angle — THE REAL RACE might between the bad-token and good-token connections IN THE HTTP LAYER:

The `connect()` helper retries up to 200 times every 5ms — that's for the server coming up. In the E4 test the sequence is:

1. `runWireServe` future started (boot in progress, handler not attached).
2. Bad-token `WebSocket.connect` — TCP accepted (Dart accepts connections on bind), request buffered in HttpServer stream (handler not attached yet). Client awaits response.
3. Boot completes → serve closure → `httpListen` attaches → buffered bad-token request delivered → 401 → client throws → expectLater passes.
4. Good-token `connect()`: attempt 1 → `WebSocket.connect` → TCP connect, upgrade request → handler → tokenOk → `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade` → returns ws. → hello sent → welcome expected.

Where can 10s pass without welcome? Scenarios:

**Scenario A: the buffered-request delivery order.** Dart's HttpServer stream delivers buffered events. Hmm.

**Scenario B: `_attaching` stuck true.** If a FIRST attach got as far as `_attaching = true` but its frame stream never delivered a hello AND never errored... then `_client == null && _attaching == true` → the good-token attach would get `already_attached`! And the client would... wait, the client's `ws.first` would receive the `already_attached` error frame — NOT welcome. The test expects `decodeLine(first)['kind'] == 'welcome'` — it would FAIL immediately with a wrong-kind assertion, not a 10s timeout. But the review says it dies at the `.timeout(10s)` on `ws.first` — meaning NO frame at all arrived in 10s.

Hmm wait, actually — if the good connect got `already_attached` before its handshake, the frame WOULD arrive (an error frame), and `ws.first` would complete with that frame → the expect on 'welcome' fails → test fails but NOT via timeout. The review explicitly says it dies at `ws.first.timeout(10s)`. So no frame arrived at all within 10s.

What yields NO frame within 10s?
- The good-token `WebSocket.connect` succeeded (otherwise the helper would have retried or fail() after 200 attempts... wait — if all 200 attempts failed, `fail()` throws a TestFailure — different failure). So ws was returned: the upgrade completed → `server.attach` was called → `httpListen` handler ran the upgrade → `attach()` executed. In attach, either:
  - `_shutDown` → sends `shutting_down` frame (arrives → not a timeout).
  - `already_attached` branch → sends error frame (arrives → not a timeout).
  - Normal: `_attaching = true; frames.listen(...)`. The welcome comes only when the HELLO frame is processed via `_onClientFrame`.

So for a pure timeout: attach took the normal path, but the client's hello never reached `_onClientFrame` within 10s, OR `_sendSafely(welcome, send)` never made it to the socket.

The client sent hello AFTER `WebSocket.connect` returned (upgrade complete → server called `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade` → returns ws → `attach()` called synchronously after). Wait — ordering: in `httpListen`, `upgrade(request)` is awaited; then `attach(decodeNdjson(server, ws.cast<Object>(), send), send)`.

`decodeNdjson` is a `messages.map(...).where(...)` — a lazy transform of the ws stream. `attach` calls `frames.listen(...)` — this listens to the transformed stream, which listens to the ws stream. Since `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade` already returned, the server-side ws is a full duplex WebSocket; events after listen flow.

Client: after `connect()` returns, `ws.add(jsonEncode(hello))`. Frame goes over the socket → server ws delivers → decodeNdjson → map → `_onClientFrame` → welcome sent back.

For the welcome to never arrive in 10s: maybe the server-side event loop was BLOCKED (in-process test! `runWireServe` runs in the same process/isolate as the test). If the boot path does something CPU-heavy or awaits something that never completes WITHOUT yielding... no — boot completed (serve closure ran, since attach got called... wait, did it?).

Hold on — actually, did attach even get called? What if the good-token connect() helper's FIRST attempt hit the server when the handler was NOT yet attached? Then the request is buffered; `WebSocket.connect` awaits the response; it would complete once the handler attaches (boot finished) — with a 101. That's fine, just delayed.

Alternatively, the helper's attempt got the 401!! WAIT. Here's a nasty one: what if there are TWO upgrade requests in flight — the bad one and the good one — and the HTTP server delivers them in order: bad → 401, good → 101. Sequential in the test, so no.

Hmm, but what about the `ws.first` — after `ws.first` gets the welcome, subsequent... no, the failure IS the timeout.

I could try `dmtools` or the GitHub API to get logs. Let me try fetching the run's failed job log. Actually — maybe easier: run the test locally in a loop and see if it flakes. That's the TDD "RED" step: reproduce.

tags:
  integration:
    # Integration tests spawn real processes / network and are excluded from the
    # pre-commit gate. Run them manually with: dart test --tags integration
  browser-ext:
    # Headless-Chrome extension suite (test/browser_ext/). CI runs it only
    # through the dedicated browser-ext.yml workflow (builds sw/agent.js and
    # supplies Chrome for Testing); ci.yml's tag job excludes it:
    # dart test --tags integration --exclude-tags browser-ext
  llm:
    # Real-provider smoke tests (issue #551): hit live provider APIs and need
    # secrets. They carry `integration` too and run ONLY in the tag-only
    # provider-smoke job (v* tags) and nightly — every per-PR suite excludes
    # them: dart test --exclude-tags llm
    #
    # gh-1199: the boundary is now enforced at the gate's integration shard
    # SELECTION too (shard_files.py --exclude-tag llm, asserted by
    # test/scripts/shard_files_llm_boundary_test.dart) and by
    # scripts/check_llm_tag_boundary.py — a live-looking integration file
    # without this tag fails the static gate. See docs/live-llm-testing.md.
    #
    # Rate limiting (issue #931 part 3.3): package:test forbids `concurrency`
    # in tag overrides (test_core _disallow('concurrency') for tag scopes, v1.32),
    # so the pin lives on the CI invocations: the per-PR integration shards run
    # `--concurrency=4`, which bounds concurrent live-provider tests PER JOB at
    # 4 (they previously ran at the default = CPU count). gh-1005 (2026-09-30)
    # retired the mac leg: the per-PR suite runs ONCE (pty-integration-linux,
    # 3 shards x 4 = 12 concurrent live tests) and nightly's unsharded leg
    # runs hours later — the old mac+linux same-window doubling (24) is gone.
    # If provider 429s start flaking the leg, lower the knob; per-job rate
    # pinning across CI jobs has no native Actions primitive.
  pty:
    # Child-agent-spawn PTY tests (issue #553): the test drives a full task
    # tool spawn — a second CLI process whose boot/JIT time is unbounded on a
    # loaded runner. They carry `integration` too and run in the per-PR
    # sharded legs (the shard manifest includes them — bounded
    # --concurrency, prewarmed boots) and nightly; the no-key
    # integration-mock leg still excludes them: dart test --exclude-tags pty
  io:
    # IO tests use dart:io primitives (local sockets, processes) and are
    # excluded from the default pre-commit gate. Run them with:
    # dart test --tags io
  perf:
    # Perf gates (issue #262): generate large fixtures and assert open
    # budgets. Selected by --tags integration in CI; run standalone with
    # dart test --tags perf
  reg-parity:
    # omp REG parity suite (issue #810): structural diff of the committed
    # omp reference twins vs fa's pure-Dart engine renders. Fast, hermetic
    # (no PTY, no network), SKIPs when the fixtures are not captured yet.
    # Merge-blocking through the EXISTING legs: ci.yml test-core (dart test
    # runs it) and the pty-visual job (fa_omp_reg_visual_test.dart) both
    # aggregate into Quality gate; the pre-commit hook's test-core stage
    # runs the same suite, so hook/CI marker parity holds with no new
    # stage. Standalone: dart test test/cli/omp_reg_parity_test.dart

messages.preview: Let me examine the send path and the protocol acceptHello, plus check how the client-side `ws.first` interacts:

blocks.text:
Same signature: `TimeoutException` at 538:21 — `ws.first` never completed within 10s.

Now let me think about the mechanics precisely, because I need a fix that addresses the root cause.

Test code path:

```dart
final served = cli.runWireServe(
  serve: (server) => httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token'),
  onDiagnostic: (line) => stderr.writeln(line),
);
// Wrong token: [REDACTED:Sensitive Value] is refused (HTTP 401)
await expectLater(
  WebSocket.connect('ws://127.0.0.1:${http.port}?token=wrong').then<void>((_) {}),
  throwsA(anything),
).timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));
// The right token works
final ws = await connect(http.port, token: '[REDACTED:Sensitive Value]');
ws.add(jsonEncode({...hello...}));
final first = await ws.first.timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10));  // ← 538
```

Server path: `runWireServe` boots (async — `await _wireServeBoot(pumpSub)`) then calls `serve(server)` → `httpListen(http, server, 'sekrit-token')` → `http.forEach(handler)`.

Timeline analysis with `HttpServer` buffering:

1. `bindLoopback(0)` — server bound, TCP accepting (OS backlog + dart accept loop). Handler NOT attached yet.
2. Bad-token client connects. TCP accepted by dart (HttpServer accepts sockets immediately on bind — the socket is accepted and the request is parsed; the HttpRequest is added to the server stream's buffer since nobody listens yet).
3. Boot finishes (some ms). `serve` closure runs → `httpListen` → `http.forEach` attaches listener → buffered bad-token request delivered → 401 → client throws → expectLater passes.
4. Good-token connect attempt #1: if boot is done, upgrade proceeds... 

Wait — the retry helper is only needed if the server socket REFUSES. With pre-bind, connection always succeeds at TCP level. So attempt #1 awaits the handshake response — which comes once the handler processes the request. All sequential. The upgrade should succeed, `attach` runs, hello → welcome.

So how can `ws.first` hang for 10s with NO frame?

**Critical: `http.forEach` processes requests SEQUENTIALLY.** `Stream.forEach` waits for the async callback per event. So:

- Request A (bad token): handler starts. `tokenOk` fails → `response.statusCode = 401; await response.close()`. Quick. Done.
- Request B (good token): handler: tokenOk passes → `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade(request)` → ws → `attach(...)` → returns done.future (held until detach).

Hmm wait — `forEach` awaits the callback... The callback for request B awaits `server.attach(...).whenComplete(ws.close)` — i.e., the WHOLE client session. That means `http.forEach` stays pending until the client detaches. Fine — `listenDone` just hangs until shutdown; the serve closure races it with `shutdown.future`.

OK so sequencing-wise B's handler only STARTS after A's handler COMPLETES. If A's handler hangs (e.g., `await request.response.close()` never completes), B never gets processed → B's client handshake never gets a response → `connect()` helper: attempt #1's `WebSocket.connect` hangs forever (NOT an exception — so no retry, no fail) → `await connect(...)` at line 530 would hang — but the failure was at line 538, meaning `connect()` RETURNED. So the upgrade DID complete for B. Attach DID run (or did it?).

Wait — `connect()` returning means `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade` completed on the server (that's what produces the 101 response the client awaits). And `attach` is called immediately after the upgrade in the same handler. So `attach()` was called: either it took the `_shutDown` path, the `already_attached` path, or the normal path.

- `already_attached` path: sends an error FRAME → client would receive it → `ws.first` completes with `already_attached` → assertion fails (not timeout). NOT our case (we have a pure timeout).
- `_shutDown` path: sends `shutting_down` frame → same as above. NOT our case.
- Normal path: `_attaching = true`, `frames.listen(...)` on `decodeNdjson(server, ws.cast<Object>(), send)`.

In the normal path, the welcome is sent only when the client's HELLO is decoded and delivered to `_onClientFrame`. The client DID `ws.add(hello)` right after connect. For no frame to come back within 10s:

**Possibility 1: The server-side WS never delivered the hello to the decodeNdjson stream.** Why? The `ws.cast<Object>()` + `map` + `where` — `attach` listens immediately after `upgrade` returns. Events can't be lost (single-subscription stream buffers). Hmm.

**Possibility 2: The server never got the hello because the CLIENT never sent it.** The client's `ws.add(...)` right after `WebSocket.connect` resolves... `WebSocket.add` queues the frame for delivery. No reason to stall.

**Possibility 3: THE WELCOME WAS SENT BUT INTO THE WRONG SINK / the client was connected to a DIFFERENT (stale) server.** Hmm! Wait — in-process, each test boots its own AgentCli and binds its own port. E4's port is fresh (`bindLoopback(0)`).

**Possibility 4: The event loop was blocked.** Something in the process hogging the single thread >10s. CI log timeline: E4 started ~00:36:01.14 (right after IT-3 at 00:36:01.138). Failed 00:36:11.189. If the isolate's event loop were blocked, the `.timeout` wouldn't fire either... it did fire exactly at 10s. So the event loop was alive. The dart test runner runs tests concurrently (--concurrency=4 within this suite — other tests running simultaneously). The event loop being alive means timers fire. So the server's async machinery had CPU — but the welcome still didn't arrive.

**Possibility 5 — THE BIG ONE: the `connect()` helper stacked connections.** Here's the thing I dismissed: WHEN does `WebSocket.connect` throw? On connection-refused or bad response. The port is pre-bound, so connect at TCP always succeeds... BUT what about a request sent BEFORE the handler attached? The client awaits the response — buffered server-side. Not an exception.

BUT WAIT — look at the FIRST E4 phase (bad-token expectLater): `WebSocket.connect(...).then<void>((_) {})` — expected to throw. What if the server responds 101?! No — tokenOk fails for 'wrong'... `tokenOk(request, 'sekrit-token')` with `?token=wrong` → false → 401. OK.

Hmm, hold on. What if the bad-token request's 401 response races the client such that `WebSocket.connect` throws NOT because of 401 but because the socket closed? Either way it throws → expectLater passes.

**Possibility 6: `_attaching` got STUCK true → good-token attach → `already_attached` → but the frame WAS sent... to the client...** — we ruled that out because the client would receive the error frame and `ws.first` would complete (test would fail on the expect, not timeout). UNLESS the error frame send FAILS or the frame never reaches the client because... hmm, `_sendSafely`? Let me look at `_sendSafely` — maybe it swallows errors. But the socket is a fresh upgrade; sending works.

Hmm wait, actually let me re-examine: is it possible that `connect()` retried MULTIPLE times, with earlier attempts creating GHOST attaches? So where's the flake? Let me think about the bad-token request arriving BEFORE `httpListen` attaches. In Dart, `HttpServer` is a single-subscription stream. Requests that arrive before `listen` — I need to check Dart's behavior: does `HttpServer` buffer them? If the server receives a request before the listener attaches, the connection is accepted at the OS level and the HttpRequest object is created, but the stream events... `HttpServer` implements `Stream<HttpRequest>`; events emitted before listen are buffered (standard single-subscription stream semantics). So they get delivered when `forEach` (which calls listen) attaches. OK.

Now the retry helper: it retries when `WebSocket.connect` THROWS. With the port pre-bound, does `WebSocket.connect` ever throw before the handler attaches? The TCP connection is accepted by the OS (backlog), and Dart's HttpServer accepts the socket into its internal connection pool even before listen (I believe connections are accepted immediately upon bind; requests are only delivered via the stream once listened... hmm, actually I'm not 100% sure whether Dart accepts sockets before listen — the accept loop is wired in `bind`).

Regardless: the client's WS handshake request gets a response only after the handler processes it. Until then, `WebSocket.connect` awaits. No throw → no retry. So stacking only if requests FAIL fast. Connection-refused can't happen (port bound). So the "stacking" hypothesis is questionable...

Where can 10s pass without welcome? Scenarios:

1. The E4 test sequence:

   - Good-token `connect()` retry helper → upgrade OK → `attach()` → hello → welcome.

2. Where can "welcome never arrives in 10s" happen?

Let me think HARD about the buffering question. In Dart, `HttpServer.bind()` — after bind, the server starts accepting connections IMMEDIATELY (the accept loop is wired at bind time in the C++/event code). HTTP requests that arrive before a listen handler is attached are... Actually I recall dart:io's HttpServer is a `Stream<HttpRequest>`. Before `listen` is called, events (requests) arriving on a single-subscription stream are BUFFERED. Yes — HttpServer detaches into _HttpServer which implements Stream; incoming requests are added to the stream's internal buffer until a subscriber attaches. I'm fairly confident requests buffer rather than being dropped.

BUT — there's a subtlety: WebSocket CONNECT handshake requires the client to send the upgrade request AND wait. Client waits → fine, server responds when handler attaches.

OK here's another race candidate I should examine — **the bad-token client's socket half-close racing the server's request routing**. When the WS client gets the 401, dart:io throws `WebSocketException: Connection to 'ws://...' was not upgraded to websocket`. The client socket closes. Server: `await request.response.close()` completes. No server-side damage.

Hmm, so let me think about what ELSE could delay `welcome` by >10s in CI.

**Critical insight candidate:** `attach()` sets `_attaching = true` and listens to `decodeNdjson(server, ws.cast<Object>(), send)`. `decodeNdjson` is `messages.map(...).where(...)`. `attach` does `frames.listen(...)`. Now — WHEN does the server process the client's hello? The client sends hello AFTER `WebSocket.connect` resolves on the client side. Server side: `WebSocketTransformer.upgrade(request)` resolved → `attach` called → listen. Both sides' deliveries should proceed.

**What if `attach` never got called because the handler was still awaiting the FIRST (bad-token) request?** No — handlers run per-request independently; `http.forEach` invokes the handler for each request without waiting for the previous handler (forEach awaits the callback though! `http.forEach` — that's `Stream.forEach`, which WAITS for the async callback to complete before processing the NEXT stream event!). 

WAIT. THIS IS IT. `http.forEach((request) async {...})` — `Stream.forEach` processes events SEQUENTIALLY: it awaits the callback for each event before delivering the next. So if the bad-token request's handler is still awaiting something, the good-token request's handler START is BLOCKED.

But the bad-token handler completes quickly (401 + close). Unless... the buffered request ordering. Hmm, still fast.

Let me reconsider. What if the bad-token `WebSocket.connect` request arrives while the handler IS attached, and completes with 401 — fine. What if it arrives BEFORE handler attach — buffered; when attached, processed → 401 — fine.

Same signature: `TimeoutException` at 538:21 — `ws.first` never completed within 10s.
